newsitem.title: UK: Fear of overdrive, not BOJ, reins in dlr--analysts.
newsitem.headline: Fear of overdrive, not BOJ, reins in dlr--analysts.

text.p: The dollar may have stalled against the yen this week after hitting a 56-month high last Thursday, but this seems to be because the market is unhappy about the pace of the dollar's recent rally and not its level.
The term "intervention fears" has been cited regularly by traders and analysts as a reason for dollar/yen's halt.
But many say that although the market has not dismissed the possibility of Bank of Japan dollar-selling intervention as a myth, this is not the main factor capping the U.S. currency.

"The (dollar's) coming off is actually due to the pace of the move rather than unhappiness with the underlying direction... It's just that there's been a very rapid dollar appreciation," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe.
Dollar/yen posted a fresh multi-year high nearly every day last week, with the U.S. currency benefiting from the healthiness of America's economy and expectations of higher interest rates there.
This took the dollar to a peak of 127.19 yen last Thursday, before it subsided to 125.60 in European afternoon trade by Wednesday.
Senior Japanese officials have become increasingly vociferous in their warnings about "excessive moves" in currency markets and of central bank intervention.

Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Japanese finance ministry's international finance bureau, said in a speech to currency dealers on Wednesday that the yen's recent moves were clearly excessive and that Japan would intervene when "we think we can win".

While such comments have often served to dent the dollar slightly as they did on Wednesday, analysts say economic fundamentals favour the dollar so much that intervention, verbal or otherwise, would not be able to rein in the bulls for long.

"Ultimately the market will test the resolve of the Bank of Japan because fundamentals still argue for the dollar to go higher. But the market's not going to do that without new factors which would cause it to test them," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS here.
Dealers said there was little appetite to test the BOJ's resolve so close to an informal G7 finance ministers' meeting at the end of this month.

The basics for dollar strength are still in place, analysts said, notably the huge gap between yields to be gleaned from U.S. and Japanese assets. While 10-year U.S. Treasury notes have a yield of 6.89 percent, their Japanese counterparts have 2.15.
However, the market is unable to shake off the niggling feeling that the dollar may have come too far too fast.

"There does seem to have been a tendency for the market to get carried away by the yield gap factor... and there's the feeling Japanese government bond yields have dropped too far," said Junpei Yamamoto, head of foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in London.

Analysts acknowledge the truth in Japanese officials' verbal intervention, for example, Sakakibara's comment that the market is too pessimistic about the Japanese economy which he described on Wednesday as being very healthy.

"Sakakibara can't say rates will go up without upsetting the markets, but he is saying the market should think about the future course of the economy," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IBJ International.

Regarding intervention, some said although there was the possibility of classic intervention in which the Bank of Japan would meet the market head-on as it drives the dollar higher, the BOJ might push the dollar down by choosing a moment when the currency was falling and add momentum with its own sales.
"You can interpret his (Sakakibara's) comment as saying that is what they plan to do," BOT-Mitsubishi's Yamamoto said.
"For example, if there's data showing the US-Japan trade gap has widened, that would bring dollar/yen down and there's a possibility the BOJ would sell into that," he said.
Heightened tension over Japan's politically sensitive trade surplus with the U.S. is seen as a dollar/yen-negative factor, especially if it continues to widen as many expect.
Japan is due to announce March trade data on Wednesday. The U.S. will release its February trade figures on Thursday.
